rows.en: The most anthropomorphic passages of Scripture are the visions in the book of Ezekiel, which are known by the name Ma'aseh Merkavah [the Work of the Chariot]. Expounding those visions was a matter with which the sages occupied themselves. But they did not expound them before the multitude, nor in a gathering of colleagues and disciples, and it was a rule that one does not expound the Chariot unless one is a sage who understands of his own knowledge (Ḥagigah 2:1). For they held that a corruption of belief is not as dangerous when people believe the words as they are written as it is dangerous if such sublime matters are handed over to those of short understanding. For anthropomorphism is dangerous because it leads to idolatry, and this danger had already been overcome since the days of the exile, for since then the belief in the God of Israel had taken root in the nation, and they recognized His unity and His special providence; but speculative inquiry could bring them to the opinions of the Greek philosophers, which were dangerous to the belief in the essence of God, and to believe, as many of them believed, that God and the world are one. Of the midrash of Ma'aseh Merkavah we have only broken remnants. It was called "the secrets of the Holy One, blessed be He" and also "the secrets of the Torah" (Pesaḥim 119a). By the name "secrets of the Holy One, blessed be He" they also called the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel (Megillah 3a), and there is no other reason to call it by this name except that Jonathan in his Targum expounds the Work of the Chariot; therefore his Targum will serve us as a partial example of the character of the midrash of the Chariot. Now Jonathan hints that the vision of the Chariot is not to be taken in a material way, as a real sight, but that the prophet's seeing was in a prophetic vision, and the sight is a vision of the glory of the Shekhinah (Ezekiel 1:1); and when it is God's will to let His prophets hear the word of prophecy, a voice goes forth from heaven (ibid. 25); and all the images that were shown to him in his vision were formed for the moment and engraved in his imagination. And where he sees the hands of a man under the wings of the living creatures, and the face of a lion on the right and the face of the ox on the left, the Targum hints deliberately that these images were made for living creatures that he imagined he saw (ibid. 8, 10). With these small hints the Targum strips the garment of anthropomorphism from the Work of the Chariot, and holds that in this vision the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed to him sublime spiritual matters in sensory images to which man is accustomed in the material world. And Ben Sira said well (49:8) of the visions of God that Ezekiel saw, that the Holy One, blessed be He, showed him His glory in the Chariot; and accordingly the removal of anthropomorphism is part of the midrash of the Chariot. Despite all the warnings they gave not to expound the Chariot, there were at all times sages who occupied themselves with expounding it, and so the images in the prophet's words became matter for the imagination to set up towers flying in the air. And that, despite all this, only small traces remained in the books of the Oral Torah was because most of the masters of halakhah had no satisfaction in the masters of secret lore and did not occupy themselves with the secrets of the Torah. But the masters of secret lore, who "please themselves in the children" [Isaiah 2:6] of the soul's fancies, were at that time chiefly the sect of the Essenes. Already then they had secret writings, and they occupied themselves with the study of the angels, prophesied and interpreted dreams (Josephus), and expounded on the existence of God and on the creation of the world (Philo). From this it appears that the core of their occupation was the Work of the Chariot and the Work of Creation. Some remnants of their teaching were brought up in the book of Enoch; and after this sect came to an end, and some of its members joined others and their remnant went up among the Pharisees from whom they had come out, then too some of their secrets came out into the light, and a few remnants of them have survived for us in the Talmud (Jellinek, introduction to *Beit ha-Midrash*, part 3, XX, XXI). But inquiry into such subtle speculations brought about the opposite of what they wanted. For first and foremost they wanted to understand the spiritual matter hidden in the secret of the images, and instead the imagination bore in them new images by the thousand, and beliefs came forth that are hard to reconcile with the opinions of the Torah and the Prophets.

The four-letter name of God, YHWH, which is also called the Shem ha-Meforash [the Explicit Name],{v1_12_03:1} they held holy and did not pronounce by its letters. From the death of Simeon the Just even the priests refrained from blessing with the Name. Whoever pronounces the Name has no share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin ch. 10), and only for a great purpose did they pronounce it (Avodah Zarah 18a); therefore they gave it various substitute names. The usual substitute is "the Holy One," and they added to it the phrase "blessed be He." The epithet "Holy" as a special substitute name is found in Scripture (Job 6:10; Habakkuk 3:3). The author of the book of Enoch uses this substitute name most often. The abstract name Shekhinah is a substitute name signifying the nearness of God to a place, a person or a nation. Therefore, insofar as He watches over, protects, or pours out His spirit upon something, He is called Shekhinah. Hence they translated "the eyes of the Lord" as "the face of the Shekhinah" (Isaiah 1:15), and the Temple was translated "the house of His Shekhinah" (ibid. 5:5); and the Shekhinah protects (ibid.), and it rests [upon them], and it went into exile with Israel, and people enter under its wings. Insofar as He is the master of strength and power, He is called Gevurah [the Might]: "the hand of the Lord" is translated "the might of the Lord"; and they said "the right hand of the Might," "the mouth of the Might." God is called Makom [the Place] because His existence is in every place (Philo); and the later sages of the midrash said: because the Holy One, blessed be He, is the place of the world (Genesis Rabbah 69), or because in every place where the righteous are, He is found with them (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 35). The early sages used this substitute name mostly when they spoke of the fulfilment of His will or of its opposite, as: "the will of the Place," "the anger of the Place," "they angered the Place," "asks for reward from before the Place," "punished before the Place," "the Place desires," "those known to the Place." Shamayim [Heaven] is also an old substitute name, and it is found with Antigonus of Sokho. It is usual when God is described in His kingship, whose yoke, fear and kingdom are upon man; so we find "the kingdom of Heaven," "the fear of Heaven," "the awe of Heaven." When they spoke of His goodness towards Israel, they call Him by the name "Father in Heaven"; and they lift their eyes to their Father in Heaven. The relation of God to Israel has been described from of old as the relation of a father to his son. And since God is called Lord, as against His people, who are called servants of the Lord, He is therefore described by the substitute name Ribbona Alma [Lord of the World] (Targum Jonathan, Isaiah 3:1), and in common speech Ribbono shel Olam. And when they spoke of God as the Former and Creator of all, they called Him by the epithet "He who spoke and the world came into being." These substitute names give a picture of their belief in a spiritual unity far from anthropomorphism, and they were founded on the belief in the creation of the world by the word of God, in His providence, His power and His goodness, and that He rules over all, and in reward and punishment. These beliefs are the roots of the substitute names mentioned, but in the course of time they became like proper names of God.

The creation of the world is called Ma'aseh Bereshit [the Work of Creation]. Inquiry into it was in their eyes a dangerous thing, and many sages refrained from entering into it (Ḥagigah 2:1), and they warned that one must not expound what is above and what is below, what is before and what is after. Nevertheless, midrashim on this subject have survived, and from them we learn their opinions on the creation of the world. They believed in the creation of something from nothing. A certain philosopher said to Rabban Gamaliel (the Second): "Your God is a great artist, but He found good materials" — namely tohu and bohu, darkness, wind, water and the deeps; and Rabban Gamaliel answered him with a rebuke and said to him: of all of them "creation" is said (Genesis Rabbah 1). Had one of the sages of Israel thought so, he would not have rebuked him so sharply; surely they believed from of old in creation of something from nothing. The images of the Scriptures they took literally, and from this arose astonishing opinions, and they thought that the world is built on a material foundation. The later sages said that the Foundation Stone was at the site of the Temple (Yoma ch. 5, Bavli and Yerushalmi, and Tosefta ch. 2). In the book of Enoch he calls the foundation "a corner stone," and Enoch reached the foundation and saw the corner stone (18:2). Light is a spark of the radiance of the splendor of the Holy One, blessed be He (Ben Sira 43:2), and this is not a poetic figure but words meant literally; and one of the masters of aggadah testifies that he received this from his predecessors and that it was handed to him in a whisper (Genesis Rabbah 3). For most natural phenomena they gave astonishing causes that have no natural relation to the effect. Examples of the lore of the Work of Creation of the early sages, the masters of the Mishnah, the Talmuds and the midrashim, are found in scattered places in the two Talmuds and in the books of midrash;{v1_12_04:1} but they are not many, because they were careful about expounding it and publishing it in public. From the remnants that are in our hands we understand that it is the inquiry into the creation of the world and of the things that exist, according to what they drew out of the section of the Work of Creation or out of verses in the rest of Scripture that speak of God's works in the nature of the creatures. The ancients had a complete book of this kind, called *Sefer Yetzirah* and also *Hilkhot Yetzirah*. We also have a *Sefer Yetzirah*, which is not the *Sefer Yetzirah* of the early masters of the Talmud (see *Dor Dor ve-Dorshav*, part 4, pp. 150, 218); but it too is a midrash of the Work of Creation. The later authorities disagreed on the matter. Maimonides said in his books that the matter of the Work of Creation is natural science, and most of the sages of Spain agreed with him; but Rabbenu Nissim said in his *Derashot* (sermon 1) that the Work of Creation is not natural science, for if it were, why did our sages command that it be concealed, so as not to expound it in public? Therefore he determined that besides the natural science that is acquired by the inquiry of the intellect, there is a natural science that is known only by divine influx, and that is the lore of the Work of Creation of the ancients (ibid., part 5, pp. 27, 139); and such was the opinion of the Kabbalists. Creation exists for the sake of the righteous man, etc. (Berakhot 6b; Genesis Rabbah and Tanḥuma; the book of Enoch; and 4 Ezra ch. 4); for the Holy One, blessed be He, wished His name to be magnified, and therefore He created the world (Yoma 38a), and this is fulfilled through those who do His will. The Torah was His instrument of craft in creation (Ḥagigah 12a; Genesis Rabbah 1), and it preceded the creation of the world (Pesaḥim 54a; Ben Sira ch. 1 and ch. 24); and wisdom is the Torah. Philo describes the supreme wisdom by the name "word" (logos), which was His instrument of craft in creation, and it is the spirit of the divine Torah (in the books *On Flight* 458 and *On the Cherubim* 129). The word, which is the supreme wisdom, was regarded by the Greek philosophers as a separate substance: God and the word are not one, but the word is like an emanation from the essence of God, and exists by itself in order to be the intermediary that carries out the will of God, to give life, order and motion in the material world. This is the doctrine of the logos at its root; but in the secondary notions the Greek sages differ from one another. Philo described the word as a distinct being, as though it were second to the God of the world; yet he is not like one who believes in two powers, but it is rather like a messenger carrying out his mission. Now the doctrine of the logos found those who honored it also among the Jews in the Land of Israel; but they did not enter into philosophical speculations, and in this too they relied on the holy writings. Behold, Solomon in his Proverbs describes wisdom as a being in its own right, and this wisdom is the Torah, for to them it alone is the true wisdom. So too Ben Sira describes wisdom (ch. 24): its seat is on high, it pours forth the spirit of prophecy, and it comes forth from the mouth of God Most High; and the source of wisdom is the Torah (ch. 1). From this it appears that wisdom is divine, and the word is wisdom, which is the Torah. Besides this, they regarded the divine word as a substance in its own right. From their saying that from every single word that goes forth from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, an angel is created (Ḥagigah 14a), we learn that they believed in the substantiality of the word; and elsewhere they said that where the Lord spoke with Moses "in a vision," this is a vision of speech (Sifrei Be-ha'alotkha, pisqa 103). Had this belief not been old, the later sages would not have invented such a new thing out of their own hearts. The Aramaic translators too used the word *memra* in an abstract way, as though it were a being in its own right, for in truth such was the belief. From the time when they began to strive to remove anthropomorphism, this notion of the word grew stronger, and that time preceded their knowledge of Greek wisdom; for most of the emendations of the Scribes, known and unknown, are products of this striving, and they are very old. Yet the opinion about the word was no danger to the belief in unity, just as the belief in angels was not dangerous to unity. For we have already seen above that they believed that the Holy One, blessed be He, shows the revelation of His Shekhinah in sensory images, and this by a new creation at each time of need. Therefore all the acts that depend on accidental qualities and cause a change in the agent are performed by the angels whom the Lord created for this purpose. Of this kind are the angel of the presence, the savior, of the Second Isaiah, the destroying angel of the book of Samuel, and the angel of the covenant of Malachi. And it is very likely that the doctrine of angels, which spread in the exile and afterwards, was founded at its core on the striving to remove anthropomorphism in every possible way. Now the matter is likewise with regard to the word. For if the level of their understanding was not fit to grasp abstract and philosophical notions, their belief came to their aid: they believed that all the acts and qualities ascribed to God are His angels, who do His will, and in this category is also the word. For this reason the philosophical notion of the Alexandrians about the word found favor in the eyes of the sages of the Land of Israel, because it agreed with their belief. But they did not turn to the speculations and the consequences that were attached to it; it was enough for them to know that Greek wisdom agrees with their belief. Now as for the translators' use of the word *memra* in an abstract way, as though it were a being in its own right, this is not an opinion taken from the Greeks; it is an opinion native to the Jews, and the translators did not originate it in order to teach the people the removal of anthropomorphism. On the contrary: long before, the belief that God is not corporeal had taken root in the people, and in agreement with this Jewish belief the translators made their translations. However, there is a great difference between the notion of the word among the Jews in the Land of Israel and the notion of it among the Greeks. For to the Greeks the word was at the rank of divinity, and in Philo's opinion it is second to the God of the world and something like an intermediary between God and the material world; but the word among the Jews was a created thing, at the rank of an angel doing His will, and it is the divine wisdom, which in their opinion is the Torah; therefore the word is the Torah, and in this there is agreement between the Pharisees in the Land of Israel and Philo.

In the manner of creation there is a likeness between the images of Philo and those of the sages of the Land of Israel. In Philo's opinion the world was first created in thought, and according to this thought — which is the spiritual image formed in the soul of the thinker — He created the material world (in the book *On the Creation of the World* 3). Close to this is also the opinion of the sages of the Oral Torah, who compare creation to the building of a palace: as the craftsman looks at the plans he has, to know how he is to make the rooms, so the Holy One, blessed be He, looks into the Torah and builds the world (Genesis Rabbah 1; ⚠1 4). The root of this midrash is hinted at in the dispute of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel: the House of Shammai say, the thought was at night and the deed by day, and the House of Hillel say, both by day (Genesis Rabbah 12); and according to both of them, thought came first. But on this matter there are only obscure hints, for the sages of the Land of Israel guarded themselves from entering into speculation on "what is before." With regard to time, the opinions of the Greeks are known: that time is eternal, or that it came into being with being and existence, without which the notion of time cannot be pictured, and that the six days of creation in the Torah are not to be taken literally (Philo); but for the sages of the Land of Israel time was one of the created things (4 Ezra 5:49), and the aggadot about the things that were created before the creation of the world point to this opinion, for these aggadot necessarily presuppose the existence of time. And one of the later sages said that there was an order of times before (Genesis Rabbah 3), and one must not take his words out of their plain meaning, as his commentators did, for we have seen that such was the prevailing opinion in the Land of Israel. The noble part of creation is man. They believed that for his sake the world was created, and that he was created in the image of God. And the expression "image of God" was not understood in a corporeal way. For the aggadah tells that the Seventy changed [the text] and wrote: "I will make man in an image and in a likeness" instead of "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness" (Mekhilta Bo 14 and in many places); from this it appears that "in our image, after our likeness" was understood only of the spiritual quality. Therefore the later sages said that there are people who are in His image and likeness and there are those who are not in His image and likeness (Genesis Rabbah 8); and their meaning is that image and likeness were said of the spiritual quality, and the righteous possess the image of God and the wicked do not. Therefore the image of God is a figure for the soul. And they believed that the soul is a spiritual being, existing by itself in a special place in heaven (Ḥagigah 12b); and when the body is formed in the mother's womb, the Holy One, blessed be He, puts a soul into it (Niddah 31a). In its first place it is pure (Berakhot 60b); in its joining with the body it becomes soiled (Shabbat 152b). Therefore it would have been better for man not to have been created than to have been created (Eruvin 13b), for by his creation the soul was turned away from its purity because of sin; therefore let a man take care to keep his soul pure (ibid.). This keeping lies in man's will, and to him the freedom is given to follow his good inclination or his evil one (Ben Sira 15:14; Sifrei Re'eh, pisqa 53; and in the Gemara in many places). The moral good that a man should choose is the fear of Heaven in general (Avot 1:3). Fear is the beginning of love (Ben Sira ch. 25), and the fruit of the fear of Heaven is the fear of sin (Berakhot 19a; Avot ch. 2, ch. 3, and in many places). The greatest of the merits is the study of Torah (Pe'ah 1:1; Ben Sira 6:36–38), and second to it are the Temple service and acts of loving-kindness; these three were counted as the pillars of the world (Avot ch. 1).

rows.en: The value of Torah study is great if it leads to deeds (Avot ch. 1), and meditating on it is not enough; rather, keeping it is the main thing (Ben Sira 6:38). But the performance of the commandments is not acceptable when it is done without intention (Berakhot 2:1), and a man's deeds in general should be for the sake of Heaven (Avot ch. 2), whether eating and drinking (Beitzah 16a) or his other affairs (Tobit, in many places); and the condition of the deed is faith: faith that the Torah is from Heaven (Sanhedrin 10:1), faith in the faithful shepherd, who is Moses (Mekhilta Beshallaḥ 6), and in the prophets of the Lord (2 Chronicles 20). Whoever performs a commandment in faith, great is his reward (Mekhilta ibid.); and as a reward for faith in Him who commanded Moses to perform the signs and wonders, the Holy One, blessed be He, performs miracles and mighty deeds for them (Mekhilta de-Amalek 1; Rosh Hashanah 29a; ⚠1 16); by the merit of faith they were redeemed from Egypt (Mekhilta Beshallaḥ 3), and by its merit the exiles are gathered in (ibid. 6). The commandments were divided into two parts: commandments between man and God, and commandments between man and his fellow. The first principle of the first part is the acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven (in many places), and in it are included the virtue of giving thanks both for the good and for the bad (Berakhot ch. 9); the justification of Heaven's judgment (Sifra, the opening of Millu'im; Ta'anit 8a); serving the Lord out of love (Sotah 24a;⚠2 Sifrei Va-etḥanan, pisqa 32), and awakening the love of all who come into the world for the Holy One, blessed be He (Sifrei ibid.); and the love must not be for the sake of receiving reward (ibid., pisqa 41), but, like the service of the Lord in general, it should be only for the sake of its own working (ibid., Ekev, pisqa 48), not on condition of receiving reward (Avot ch. 1). Love is carried into deed by cleaving to the ways of the Lord (Sifrei, pisqa 49) and by being like Him: as He is merciful and gracious, so shall man be (ibid., and Mekhilta de-Shirah 3; Yerushalmi Pe'ah ch. 1; and Shabbat 133b); and by keeping His commandments, without distinguishing between a light commandment and a grave one (Avot ch. 2; Sifrei Re'eh, pisqa 79 and 82). The greatest in this part of the commandments is the commandment of the sanctification of the Name: it is a man's duty to give up his life and his means to sanctify the Name (Sifrei Va-etḥanan, pisqa 32). The principle "Give yourself up and sanctify My Name!" (Sifra Emor 9) was held fast by the Jews at all times. But before the destruction it was kept with greater strictness than after it. Formerly they gave up their lives for every light transgression, but in the upper chamber of the house of Nitzah in Lydda they were somewhat more lenient. The commandments between man and his fellow are all the commandments of justice and uprightness, mercy and grace, and the foundation of them all is the love of man for man, which includes acts of loving-kindness, which are a pillar of the world. The root of this foundation is: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow" (Tobit 4:16); this is the whole of the Torah, and all the rest is only like its commentary (Shabbat 31a); and they called this rule "a great principle in the Torah" (Sifra Kedoshim 4). One of the great merits is the giving of charity, and it was counted as part of acts of loving-kindness; and the two together are weighed against all the commandments (Yerushalmi Pe'ah ch. 1); and whoever does much loving-kindness is praiseworthy (the book of Tobit, in many places). It is a ransom for the sinning soul (Daniel 4:24), and its reward is in this world and in the World to Come (Pe'ah ch. 1), and it is one of the marks by which Israel are distinguished (Yevamot 79a). Acts of loving-kindness are for the living, healthy and sick, and also for the dead, to bury them according to their honor (Tobit, in many places; Mekhilta de-Amalek 2; and in the Gemara in many places). Belonging to love and to acts of loving-kindness is also the duty of rebuke, for they believed that all Israel are sureties for one another (Shevuot 39a). Like the Torah and acts of loving-kindness, the Temple service too is one of the pillars of the world. Therefore the early pietists longed to bring a sacrifice (Nedarim 10a), and Judah ben Bava brought a suspensive guilt-offering every day (Keritot 25a); and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai praises the generation whose prince brings an offering for his sin (Horayot 10a; Sifra). But they did not shut their eyes to the fact that this service is below the dignity of God and close to anthropomorphism. Therefore they said that its purpose is only to give good reward to those who perform it (Mekhilta Bo 15); and where it is said that the sacrifices are "a sweet savour," this is only a figure: that it is a satisfaction before Him that His will is done (Sifra in many places; Sifrei Pinḥas, pisqa 143). But a sacrifice without purity of thought does not reach its purpose (Ben Sira ch. 34; Judith ch. 16). The belief in the preciousness of the Temple service had taken root in the nation, and the enlightened, although they lessened its value relative to the Torah and acts of loving-kindness, nevertheless guarded themselves from speaking against it outright. On the contrary, they said expressly that one should not withdraw one's hand from it, for so God commanded (Ben Sira ch. 35); and where they condemn the sacrifices of the wicked (Ecclesiastes 4:17; Ben Sira 34:5), they do not condemn the service in general, but admit that it is acceptable (Ecclesiastes 5:3; Ben Sira 35:4). Included in the service of the sacrifices are the vow and the Nazirite vow. Although these too were not acceptable in the eyes of the enlightened (Ecclesiastes 5:4; Ben Sira 18:22; Nedarim 9a and the places cited there), they could not oppose them, since they had taken root in the people. Many practiced the Nazirite vow (Yerushalmi Berakhot), especially in a time of trouble (Nazir 5:1). Likewise fasting is a great merit (Tobit 11, and in the Mishnah and Talmud in many places), and in all the troubles of the community they decreed a fast (Tractate Ta'anit; 1 Maccabees 3:47; Judith 4:17). For every affliction of the soul was to them like the sacrifices and even dearer than they, since sufferings win favor more than sacrifices (Sifrei Va-etḥanan 39;⚠3 Mekhilta de-Ba-Ḥodesh 10), for sufferings scour the soul and atone (Ta'anit 21a), like death, which scours (Shevuot 8a) and atones (Sifrei Shelaḥ 112, Naso 4; Sanhedrin 43a). Yet although death atones, they were nevertheless accustomed to bring an offering to atone for the souls of the dead (2 Maccabees 12:58).⚠4

footnotes.en: Shem ha-meforash is like "proper name" [shem perati]. Every singling out is called perat, as in: "he specified (perat) the vow," "he specified the sin." Parash and parat sometimes interchange, as in: "until Scripture specifies (she-yifrot) for you" (Pesaḥim 22b), where the Yerushalmi reads "until it specifies (she-yifrosh)." Therefore it is possible that shem ha-meforash means the same as shem ha-meforat, and that is what we call a proper name.

See Ḥagigah, Bavli and Yerushalmi, at the beginning of ch. 2, and Genesis Rabbah in several places in its sections, and Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, and elsewhere in many places in the Gemara and in the midrash.
